title: Health & Safety in Engineering Manufacture
description: Risk assessment, PPE, workshop hazards and the control measures engineers use to keep people safe.
content_html:
Why Health and Safety Matters in Engineering

Engineering workshops and manufacturing facilities contain some of the most hazardous environments in any industry. Rotating machinery, sharp tools, hot materials, heavy loads, electrical equipment, and airborne particles all pose real risks to operators. Legal obligations under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 place a duty on employers to protect workers, and on employees to cooperate with safety procedures. Beyond legal compliance, good health and safety practice reduces accidents, prevents costly downtime, protects equipment, and enables engineers to focus on productive work rather than incident management.

Risk Assessment

A risk assessment is the cornerstone of engineering safety management. It follows a defined process: identify the hazard (anything with the potential to cause harm), decide who might be harmed and how, evaluate the risk (likelihood × severity), implement control measures to reduce the risk, and review the assessment regularly or when conditions change. In an engineering context, hazards might include swarf (metal chips) from turning operations, solvent fumes during finishing, or a guillotine blade during shearing. For each hazard, the engineer records the risk level and the specific control measures in place.

Risk is assessed on two dimensions: the likelihood of the hazard causing harm, and the severity of that harm if it occurs. A high-likelihood, high-severity risk (for example, unguarded rotating shafts) demands immediate and robust control. A low-likelihood, low-severity risk (for example, tripping on a cable on a well-managed shop floor) requires attention but is lower priority. The aim is never to eliminate all risk — that is rarely possible — but to reduce it to an acceptable and reasonably practicable level.

Key Fact

The five steps of risk assessment are: (1) identify the hazard, (2) decide who might be harmed and how, (3) evaluate the risk (likelihood × severity), (4) implement control measures, (5) review and update the assessment. In engineering, this process is applied to every operation involving machinery, tools or hazardous materials.

Common Hazards in Engineering Manufacture

Different manufacturing operations present different hazards. During machining (turning, milling, drilling), swarf is a major hazard — sharp metal chips can cut skin, enter eyes, or jam machinery; the rotating chuck or workpiece can catch loose clothing. During welding and brazing, UV radiation from the arc can cause permanent eye damage, fumes are toxic, and the workpiece and surrounding area reach extreme temperatures. During casting, molten metal is typically above 700 °C for aluminium and much hotter for ferrous metals, making burns a severe risk; steam can erupt if moisture is present in the mould. During finishing processes such as spray painting and powder coating, solvent fumes and fine particles are respiratory and fire hazards.

Noise-induced hearing loss is a long-term hazard from sustained exposure to machine noise above 85 dB(A). Manual handling of heavy workpieces risks musculoskeletal injury. Electrical hazards arise from power tools and machine supplies. A thorough risk assessment must account for all hazards relevant to the specific operation being carried out, not just the obvious ones.

Control measures are prioritised from most to least effective. Elimination (remove the hazard entirely) is best but often impractical in manufacturing. Substitution (replace a hazardous material or process with a safer one) is next. Engineering controls (machine guards, local exhaust ventilation, interlocks) reduce exposure without relying on human behaviour. Administrative controls (safe operating procedures, training, supervision, permit-to-work systems) rely on people following rules. PPE (personal protective equipment) is the last line of defence — it does not eliminate the hazard but protects the wearer if all other controls fail. PPE should never be the only control measure for a significant hazard.

Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)

Personal protective equipment (PPE) is selected to match the specific hazards of each operation. Eye protection (safety spectacles or a full face shield) is mandatory for all machining, grinding, welding and casting operations — swarf and sparks travel at high velocity and metal splashes are unpredictable. Hearing protection (ear defenders or earplugs) is required where noise levels exceed 85 dB(A), including near grinding machines, pneumatic tools and loud presses. Welding operations require a welding helmet or auto-darkening shield to protect against UV radiation, in addition to fire-resistant gloves and a leather apron to guard against burns and spatter. Respiratory protection (dust mask or respirator) is needed when sanding, grinding composite materials (which produce carcinogenic fibres), spray painting or powder coating.

Footwear with steel toecaps protects against dropped heavy components. Gloves protect against cuts from sharp edges — but must never be worn near rotating machinery such as a lathe or drill press, because they can be snagged, pulling the hand into the machine. This is a counter-intuitive but important safety rule that examiners frequently test.

Key Fact

PPE must be matched to the hazard: eye protection for machining/welding/casting; hearing protection above 85 dB(A); welding helmet + fire-resistant gloves + leather apron for welding; respiratory protection for composite grinding, spray painting and powder coating. Gloves must NOT be worn near rotating machinery as they risk entanglement.

Many students list PPE as the primary or only control measure when answering risk assessment questions. This will lose marks. PPE sits at the bottom of the control hierarchy — it is the last resort when engineering controls and administrative controls cannot fully eliminate the hazard. For maximum marks, describe the engineering control first (machine guard, extraction system, interlock), the administrative control second (training, SOP, supervision), and then PPE as the supplementary protection layer.
exam_tip_html: Risk assessment questions often ask you to complete a partially filled table: hazard, who is at risk, control measure. Always state a specific hazard (not just 'machinery') and a specific control measure (not just 'be careful'). For PPE questions, match the PPE precisely to the hazard — if the question is about drilling, the answer is safety spectacles to protect against swarf, not a hard hat. Remember that gloves must not be worn near rotating machinery — this is frequently tested. If asked to evaluate a risk assessment, check whether it covers all significant hazards, whether the control measures are adequate, and whether it has been reviewed recently.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A risk assessment identifies hazards, evaluates likelihood and severity, and specifies control measures — following five steps — and must be reviewed regularly or when conditions change.
  • Control measures follow a hierarchy: elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, then PPE — PPE is the last resort, not the first response.
  • PPE must be matched to the specific hazard: eye protection for machining and welding, hearing protection above 85 dB(A), welding helmet and leather apron for welding, respiratory protection for grinding composites or spray painting — and gloves must never be worn near rotating machinery.

glossary_terms.definition: The policies, procedures and practices put in place to protect workers from injury, ill health and harm in the workplace.
A systematic process of identifying hazards, evaluating the likelihood and severity of harm, and specifying control measures to reduce risk to an acceptable level.
Equipment worn by an individual to protect against health and safety risks; the last line of defence when other control measures cannot fully eliminate a hazard.
Anything in the workplace that has the potential to cause harm, injury or ill health to a person.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is correct regarding the use of gloves near a lathe?
A) Gloves should always be worn to protect the hands from swarf
B) Gloves must not be worn because they can be caught by rotating parts
C) Gloves should be worn only when the machine is running at low speed
D) Gloves are optional if the operator has more than two years' experience
practice_questions.marks: B) Gloves must not be worn because they can be caught by rotating parts [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two pieces of PPE that must be worn during a manual arc welding operation.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: welding helmet / auto-darkening shield (to protect against UV radiation) / fire-resistant gloves / leather apron (to protect against burns and spatter) / safety boots with steel toecaps. Do not accept plain safety spectacles alone as these do not protect against UV from the arc. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why PPE is described as the 'last line of defence' in the control hierarchy.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for stating that PPE does not remove or reduce the hazard itself. Second mark: it only protects the individual wearer if the hazard causes an incident — so if the PPE fails or is not worn correctly, the person is unprotected. Third mark: higher-level controls such as machine guards (engineering controls) or safe operating procedures (administrative controls) reduce the hazard for everyone, regardless of individual behaviour, and are therefore more reliable and effective. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the five steps of a risk assessment. Give one example of a control measure for the hazard of swarf during a drilling operation.
practice_questions.marks: Description (3 marks — one per step, award up to 3): identify the hazard; decide who might be harmed and how; evaluate the risk (likelihood × severity); implement control measures; review and update. Example (1 mark): for swarf during drilling — the operator must wear safety spectacles to prevent chips from entering the eyes / a swarf guard should be fitted to the pillar drill to contain chips. [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A school engineering workshop runs a risk assessment review after a student cuts their hand on swarf while removing a workpiece from the lathe. The current risk assessment only lists 'wear gloves' as the control measure for swarf.

Discuss whether this control measure is appropriate and what additional measures should be considered.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion that identifies the problem with the current measure (gloves must not be worn near rotating lathes — entanglement risk outweighs the cut risk), then discusses appropriate engineering controls (swarf brush or hook to remove chips rather than bare hands; machine guard during cutting), administrative controls (clear SOP on how to remove swarf safely; supervision; training), and PPE that is appropriate (safety spectacles to prevent chips entering the eyes, rather than gloves). The discussion acknowledges that 'wear gloves' is actively dangerous near rotating machinery — not just ineffective.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two or more relevant points developed and linked to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): Identifies that gloves are inappropriate near lathes but does not develop alternatives.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant safety point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A manufacturing company is about to introduce a new process that involves grinding carbon-fibre-reinforced polymer (CRP) components. The process will generate fine airborne particles and significant noise from the grinding machine.

Evaluate how effectively a PPE-only approach would manage the health and safety risks of this new process.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that identifies the specific hazards (fine CRP dust — carcinogenic; noise above 85 dB(A); eye hazard from particles), assesses what PPE can offer (FFP3 respirator to filter fine particles; ear defenders; safety spectacles — these address the immediate personal exposure), then critically evaluates the limitations (PPE relies on consistent correct wearing and fit; it does not remove the dust from the environment so other workers nearby are also at risk; hearing protection only works if worn at all times in the noise zone; grinding CRP is a cumulative long-term health risk where any lapse in PPE has lasting consequences). Argues that engineering controls should be primary: local exhaust ventilation (LEV) at the grinding point removes particles before they become airborne; acoustic enclosures reduce noise at source; these protect all workers regardless of individual PPE compliance. Reaches a clear substantiated judgement — PPE is necessary but insufficient alone; LEV and enclosure are essential primary controls.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both sides evaluated with some application to CRP grinding context and an attempt at judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but largely one-sided or lacking judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about PPE or hazards with little development. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is the correct reason why gloves must not be worn near a centre lathe?
options: Gloves reduce the operator's grip on the chuck key
Gloves make it harder to feel the surface finish of the workpiece
Gloves are too expensive to use routinely in a workshop
Gloves can be caught by rotating parts and pull the operator's hand into the machine

knowledge_checks.q: Where does PPE sit in the hierarchy of control measures?
options: First — it is the most effective control
Third — after administrative controls and engineering controls
Last — it is the final line of defence when other controls cannot fully eliminate the hazard

knowledge_checks.q: Noise-induced hearing loss becomes a significant risk when sustained noise exposure exceeds _____ dB(A).
In a risk assessment, risk is evaluated by considering both the _____ of the hazard causing harm and the severity of that harm.
Match each manufacturing hazard to its most appropriate PPE.
right: FFP3 respirator to filter carcinogenic fine particles
Safety spectacles to prevent chips entering the eyes

flashcard_questions.q: What are the five steps of a risk assessment?
flashcard_questions.a: Identify the hazard; decide who might be harmed and how; evaluate the risk; implement control measures; review and update the assessment.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must gloves not be worn near a lathe or drill press?
flashcard_questions.a: Gloves can be caught by rotating parts such as the chuck or drill, pulling the operator's hand into the machine and causing serious injury.
A hazard is anything in the workplace that has the potential to cause harm, injury or ill health to a person working in that environment.

flashcard_questions.q: What does PPE stand for and what is its role?
flashcard_questions.a: PPE stands for personal protective equipment; it protects the individual wearer when other control measures cannot fully eliminate a hazard.

flashcard_questions.q: State two pieces of PPE required during a welding operation.
flashcard_questions.a: A welding helmet or auto-darkening shield protects against UV radiation, and fire-resistant gloves with a leather apron protect against burns and spatter.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is PPE described as the 'last line of defence' in the control hierarchy?
flashcard_questions.a: PPE does not remove the hazard; it only protects the wearer, so if PPE is not worn correctly, the person is completely unprotected from the risk.

flashcard_questions.q: What hearing protection is required, and at what noise level does it become mandatory?
flashcard_questions.a: Ear defenders or earplugs are required when sustained noise exposure exceeds 85 dB(A), which is common near grinding machines and pneumatic tools.

flashcard_questions.q: State two hazards specific to casting operations with molten metal.
flashcard_questions.a: Molten metal at extreme temperatures causes severe burns on contact, and steam explosions can occur if moisture is present in the mould or on tools.

flashcard_questions.q: What respiratory protection is needed when grinding carbon-fibre composites?
flashcard_questions.a: An FFP3 respirator is needed to filter the fine carcinogenic particles generated when grinding carbon-fibre-reinforced polymer (CRP) components.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the first and most effective level in the hierarchy of control measures?
flashcard_questions.a: Elimination — removing the hazard entirely from the workplace — is the most effective control, as it means no one can be harmed by that hazard.

flashcard_questions.q: State two hazards associated with spray painting in a manufacturing environment.
flashcard_questions.a: Solvent fumes from spray paint are a respiratory hazard and a fire/explosion risk, especially in enclosed spaces with poor ventilation.

flashcard_questions.q: What eye protection is required when drilling metal?
flashcard_questions.a: Safety spectacles or a face shield must be worn during drilling to protect the eyes from high-velocity swarf and metal chips thrown off by the drill.
